opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say the results are mixed, and probably more modest than some of us hoped when these policies first started showing up.

The original theory of change, at least as I thought about it, was something like this: if you can get a few leading companies to voluntarily commit to "if we see these dangerous capabilities, we'll put these protections in place, and if we can't, we'll pause or slow down," you accomplish a few things at once. You show that this kind of commitment is workable and doesn't wreck a business. You build up the know-how: what the evaluations look like, what the protective measures look like, how the whole thing works in practice. And you create a template that regulators can pick up later, so that when there's political will to regulate, there's something concrete and tested to point to instead of starting from scratch.

On some of that I think there's been real progress. The vocabulary has spread. Ideas like dangerous-capability evaluations, if-then commitments, and thresholds tied to specific protections have become fairly mainstream. You see echoes of them in various government frameworks and in discussions about what reasonable safety practice looks like. Companies have had to build internal machinery for running evals and making these calls, and that machinery is a real asset if you later want to require it.

Where I'm more sobered is a couple of things. First, the commitments have often been vaguer and more flexible than I'd ideally like. There's a lot of room for interpretation, and some policies have been revised in ways that loosen them, sometimes at just the moments when you'd want them to bite. That makes them less useful as a template, because a regulator looking at them can't easily turn "we'll use our judgment" into an enforceable rule. Second, the political environment for binding regulation has been tougher than many people expected, so the "pick up the template" step hasn't really happened at the scale the theory imagined. Having a good blueprint doesn't help much if nobody's building.

So my overall take is roughly this. I think these policies were worth doing. They've moved the conversation, created infrastructure, and given us more concrete ideas about what safety practice could look like. But I don't think they've been a decisive force in making regulation happen, and I'd caution against treating them as a substitute for it. Voluntary commitments under heavy competitive pressure have real limits. They're probably most valuable as a bridge: something that keeps building knowledge and norms so that when the window for serious regulation opens, we're ready to use it well.

r001.rationale: The response says the political environment for binding regulation has been tougher than expected, making the regulatory impact more modest than hoped and preventing the template from being adopted at the imagined scale.

r002.rationale: It says company policies influenced the vocabulary and that government frameworks contain echoes of their ideas, but does not say existing or prospective regulation borrows heavily from them.

r003.rationale: It describes policies as a template and bridge for future regulation, but does not identify continually updated policies as an ongoing source of regulatory models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I've been pretty involved in this — I worked on responsible scaling policies back when I was at Open Philanthropy and then at Anthropic, so take my view with that in mind.

I think the honest answer is that it's a mixed picture, but I'd lean toward calling it a real success relative to what I was hoping for, while being clear-eyed that it hasn't gotten us anywhere close to where we'd want to be.

Let me explain what I mean. When we were first thinking about RSPs, the basic idea was: nobody actually knows what good AI regulation looks like yet. It's a very new technology, the risks are speculative in the sense that we haven't seen the catastrophic versions of them, and if you went to a legislator and said "please write a law about this," you'd get something either toothless or kind of random. So the theory was, get the companies to write down — voluntarily, publicly — what they think the dangerous capabilities are, how they'd detect them, and what they'd commit to doing if they found them. And then that becomes a kind of prototype. Regulators can look at it and say, "okay, this is what the people closest to the technology think is reasonable, now let's make it binding, let's add enforcement, let's add third-party verification."

And on that front, I think it worked better than I'd have predicted. You can draw a pretty direct line from the early RSPs to things like the EU AI Act's general-purpose model provisions, to the California frontier AI legislation, to the frameworks that various international bodies have been putting out. The vocabulary — capability thresholds, evaluations, if-then commitments — that's now just how people talk about this. That wasn't inevitable. You could imagine a world where regulation went straight to compute caps or licensing regimes or something that had no connection to actual risk assessment, and I think RSPs helped steer away from that.

Now, the critiques. The big one is that voluntary commitments are voluntary. We've seen companies loosen their frameworks when it got competitively inconvenient, we've seen a lot of vagueness about what actually triggers a pause, and we've seen very little in the way of outside verification. If your argument for RSPs is "these are a bridge to regulation," then the bridge only matters if you actually get to the other side. And I think a fair criticism is that the companies have sometimes used the existence of RSPs as an argument against regulation — "look, we're already doing this responsibly" — which is kind of the opposite of the intended effect.

The other thing I'd flag is that the race dynamics have gotten more intense than I expected, and that puts a lot of pressure on any voluntary framework. An RSP is easiest to follow when you're not that worried about being left behind. When you are, every judgment call bends in the direction of shipping.

So where does that leave me? I'd say RSPs succeeded at the "make regulation more viable" part — they gave regulators something concrete to work with and shifted the conversation toward risk-based, evidence-based approaches. Whether that viability actually gets cashed out into good, enforceable regulation is still very much an open question, and I don't think the companies can or should be the ones to answer it. That's the part that has to come from outside.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the regulatory environment was immature and could produce toothless or arbitrary rules, but does not say that this led to reduced ambitions for regulating catastrophic AI risks.

r002.rationale: It describes responsible scaling policies as prototypes for regulation and says early policies influenced major regulatory frameworks and supplied their vocabulary.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not identify continually updated policies as an ongoing source of regulatory models.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ve helped, though I’d distinguish making regulation more viable from actually getting adequate regulation in place.

One of the challenges with regulating AI is that it’s very hard to say exactly what you want companies to do. “Make sure your models are safe” isn’t a very actionable rule. And prescribing a particular set of tests forever doesn’t seem right either, because the technology is changing so quickly.

Responsible scaling policies offer a more concrete approach: identify capabilities that would create particularly serious risks, evaluate whether your systems have those capabilities, and commit in advance to safeguards you’d need before proceeding. That gives policymakers something to examine. They can ask whether the thresholds are appropriate, whether the evaluations are credible, and whether the safeguards are sufficient.

Having companies make those commitments voluntarily also helps establish that this kind of requirement is feasible. It makes the conversation less abstract and gives regulators something they can potentially build on.

But I wouldn’t equate publishing a policy with demonstrating that it works. A lot depends on the details, on whether companies follow through when doing so is costly, and on whether there’s independent scrutiny. So I’d call them useful progress toward regulation, rather than evidence that the underlying problem has been solved.

r001.rationale: The response says AI regulation is hard to specify, but does not attribute reduced ambitions for catastrophic-risk regulation to a disappointing regulatory environment.

r002.rationale: It says policymakers could build on responsible scaling policies, but does not state that existing or prospective regulation borrows heavily from them.

r003.rationale: The response notes that technology changes quickly, but does not identify continually updated responsible scaling policies as an ongoing source of regulatory models.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions. One is whether these policies have made companies behave more safely. The other is whether they’ve made it easier to imagine and implement useful regulation. I think the case for success is stronger on the second question, although there’s still a lot we don’t know.

A big challenge with regulating AI is specifying what you actually want companies to do. “Make sure your systems are safe” isn’t a very actionable requirement. Responsible scaling policies try to make that more concrete: What capabilities would trigger concern? How would you test for them? What additional security or safeguards would you need at that point? And under what circumstances would you stop scaling or deploying until you had those safeguards?

Having companies write those things down gives policymakers something they can examine, criticize, and potentially turn into requirements. It also creates an opportunity to learn which parts are practical and which parts are too vague. You don’t have to resolve every question about how dangerous future AI will be before asking companies to have a credible plan for what they’ll do if particular risks materialize.

But I wouldn’t equate publishing a policy with demonstrating that it works. The hard test is what happens when following it is costly—when a company has a commercially attractive system and the evidence about its safety is uncomfortable or ambiguous. And a voluntary policy can be changed by the company that wrote it.

So my assessment is that this has been a useful step toward making regulation more concrete and viable. It isn’t a substitute for regulation, and it isn’t yet evidence that we’ve solved the underlying safety problem.

r003.rationale: It describes the policies as a useful step, but does not identify continually updated policies as an ongoing source of regulatory models.
